mainTopic: רב and שמואל on money given to betroth one's sister, and רבינא's challenge from חלה separated from flour.
overview: The amud opens with a rule from the earlier discussion: when קידושין does not take effect, the money normally goes back. Then רב and שמואל argue about a man who gives קידושין money to his own sister. Both agree he knows it cannot work. רב says he meant it as a פקדון, so it is returned, and שמואל says he meant it as a gift, so she keeps it. רבינא challenges שמואל from a משנה: חלה separated from flour is not חלה and must be returned to the owner, so why isn't it a gift? The גמרא answers that the flour is returned for a practical reason: someone might think the dough was already fixed and come to eat טבל. It defends this answer by explaining that people know the rule but misunderstand its reason, and that people only listen to a second separation when there are two separate containers. Then it shows that the bitter cucumber case is different, because there the תרומה is real by Torah law, as רבי אלעאי learns from a פסוק. The amud ends as רבא begins a new statement, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Money from a failed betrothal is normally returned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a general rule from the earlier case: money given for a קידושין that did not work must be returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we can learn from this: in general, money given for a betrothal that did not take effect goes back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the earlier discussion by pulling out a general rule. Money given for a קידושין that failed is not a gift. It has to be given back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier case, the items given before the last one were treated as a loan that must be repaid, not as a present. From that, the גמרא concludes that this is the normal rule for failed קידושין money. This sets the background for the next מחלוקת, which deals with a special case.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it; we can conclude from this

steps.whatToRemember: Basic rule: when קידושין does not take effect, the money is given back.

phrases.english: And conclude from it:
phrases.notes: This points back to the earlier case on the daf, where the dates before the last one were treated as a loan.

phrases.english: generally, money is returned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from the previous part of the daf.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Money from a failed קידושין is normally returned, not kept as a gift.

steps.title: Betrothing one's sister: רב and שמואל disagree
steps.stepSummary: A man gives קידושין money to his sister. רב says the money must be returned, and שמואל says it is a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: if someone betroths his sister, רב says the money must be returned, and שמואל says the money is a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new מחלוקת about a man who tries to marry his own sister with money. Everyone agrees the קידושין doesn't work. The question is only what happens to the money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קידושין cannot take effect between a brother and sister, so the marriage is clearly void. רב applies the normal rule from step 1, so the money goes back. שמואל says this case is different, so she keeps the money as a gift.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces an אמוראים' disagreement)

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody here thinks the marriage works. The whole argument is only about who ends up with the money.

phrases.english: It was stated: one who betroths his sister,
Rav says: the money is returned.
And Shmuel says: the money is a gift.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the general rule to a special case where שמואל disagrees with that rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the money given to the sister is returned. שמואל: the money is a gift.

steps.title: רב's reason: he meant it as a deposit
steps.stepSummary: רב explains that the man knows קידושין cannot work with his sister, so he must have given the money as a פקדון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says the money is returned, because a person knows that betrothal does not work with his sister, so he made up his mind to give it to her as a deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב says the money goes back. The man knew all along that the קידושין was meaningless, so he must have meant something else: a deposit for her to hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the man is not fooled, the גמרא asks what he really intended. רב says he intended a פקדון, and a deposit always goes back to its owner. That is why she must return the money.

phrases.english: Rav says: the money is returned —
a person knows
that betrothal does not take effect with his sister,
and he decided to give it as a deposit.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: מָעוֹת חוֹזְרִים – אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind רב's ruling from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The man knowingly gave the money as a deposit, so it must be returned.

steps.title: Then why not just call it a deposit?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if he meant a פקדון, why didn't he say so openly?
steps.simpleTranslation: So let him tell her it is a deposit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's explanation. If the man really wanted to give a deposit, he could have just said so.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'I'm betrothing you' seems like a strange way to hand over a deposit. The question is why he would use the words of קידושין when he meant something completely different.

keyTerms.meaning: And let him say to her (a challenge: why didn't he?)

phrases.english: So let him say to her: 'as a deposit'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning given for רב in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the man meant the money as a deposit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If his intent was a deposit, the natural thing would be to say so, not to speak words of קידושין.

steps.title: She would have refused a deposit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: he thought she would not agree to accept a deposit.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought she would not accept it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. The man worried his sister would refuse to take a deposit, so he handed it over in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding a deposit is a responsibility, so someone might say no to it. By using the words of קידושין, he got her to take the money, even though he really meant it as a deposit.

phrases.english: He thought she would not accept it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the man's hidden motive for his wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed he should have openly said 'deposit.'
steps.terutzMaskana: He avoided the word because she would have refused, so רב's reading still stands.

steps.title: שמואל's reason: he meant it as a gift
steps.stepSummary: שמואל uses the same starting point. The man knows קידושין can't work with his sister, but שמואל says he meant the money as a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל holds the money is a gift, because a person knows betrothal does not work with his sister, so he made up his mind to give it to her as a gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains שמואל's side. He agrees the man knew the קידושין was meaningless, but he says the man really intended a present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both רב and שמואל agree the man is not fooled. They only disagree about what he really intended: a deposit (רב) or a gift (שמואל). A gift does not go back, so she keeps the money.

keyTerms.meaning: A person knows (assumes the man understands the law)

phrases.english: And Shmuel holds: the money is a gift —
a person knows
that betrothal does not take effect with his sister,
and he decided to give it as a gift.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל סָבַר: מָעוֹת מַתָּנָה – אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 3, now giving שמואל's reasoning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The man knowingly gave the money as a gift, so she keeps it.

steps.title: Then why not just call it a gift?
steps.stepSummary: The same question is asked of שמואל: if he meant a gift, why not say so?
steps.simpleTranslation: So let him tell her it is a gift!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל the same way it challenged רב. If he wanted to give a gift, he could have just said so.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again the problem is the wording. Why would a man use the words of קידושין if all he meant was a present?

keyTerms.meaning: And let him say (another spelling of וְלֵימָא)

phrases.english: So let him say to her: 'as a gift'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same style of challenge as step 4, now aimed at שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's claim that the man meant the money as a gift.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If his intent was a gift, he should have openly called it a gift.

steps.title: A plain gift would embarrass her
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: he thought taking a gift outright would be embarrassing for her.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thought the matter would be embarrassing for her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. The man felt an open handout would shame his sister, so he gave it in a roundabout way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking charity-like money openly can be embarrassing, so she might have said no. Using the words of קידושין let her accept it, even though he really meant it as a gift.
steps.whatToRemember: רב and שמואל agree the man knows the קידושין is void. They argue only about his real intent: a deposit that goes back (רב), or a gift she keeps (שמואל).

phrases.english: He thought: the matter is embarrassing to her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the man's hidden motive for his wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed he should have openly said 'gift.'
steps.terutzMaskana: He avoided the word to spare her embarrassment, so שמואל's reading still stands.

steps.title: רבינא's challenge from חלה separated from flour
steps.stepSummary: רבינא quotes a משנה: חלה separated from flour is not חלה, and if the כהן keeps it, it counts as stolen. By שמואל's logic it should count as a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא objects: one who separates his חלה from flour has not made real חלה, and it is stolen property in the כהן's hands. But why is it stolen? Let us say the person knows חלה cannot be taken from flour, so he gave it as a gift!
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא brings a משנה that seems to go against שמואל. A man gives a כהן 'חלה' from flour, which doesn't count, and the משנה says the כהן is holding stolen property that must go back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case looks just like the sister case. The giver should know the act is useless, so by שמואל's reasoning he meant it as a gift. Yet the משנה says the כהן has to return it, which fits רב, not שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection (from an earlier source)
The portion of dough given to a כהן
Stolen property in the כהן's hands

phrases.english: Ravina raises an objection:
one who separates his challah from flour — it is not challah,
and it is stolen property in the priest's hands.
But why is it stolen property in the priest's hands?
Let us say: a person knows
that one does not separate challah from flour,
and he gave it as a gift!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both sides were defended, רבינא attacks שמואל's reasoning from a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's principle that someone who knowingly does a void act meant to give a gift.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the חלה case the giver also should know the act is void, so by שמואל the flour would be a gift. Yet the משנה calls it stolen, which means it must be returned.

steps.title: The חלה case is different because it can lead to eating טבל
steps.stepSummary: The flour must be returned not because it is 'stolen' in the usual sense, but because leaving it with the כהן could lead him to eat untithed dough.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is different, because something harmful can come out of it. Sometimes the כהן has less than five quarters of a kav of flour. He kneads it together with this flour, thinks his dough is already taken care of, and ends up eating it as טבל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבינא's challenge from step 9. It says the חלה case has a special reason for making the כהן give the flour back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's rule that a person knowingly gives a gift still stands. The flour is called 'stolen' only so that the כהן returns it, because keeping it is dangerous. If the כהן mixes it with his own small amount of flour, the total becomes large enough to need חלה. He will think the dough is already exempt, but it is not.

keyTerms.meaning: Five quarters of a kav, the minimum amount of flour that needs חלה
His dough has been made fit to eat
Produce or dough from which the required portions have not yet been taken

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the gift idea is wrong. It is saying the חלה case has an extra concern, so the flour has to be returned anyway.

phrases.english: There it is different,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the משנה about flour-חלה that רבינא quoted in step 9.

phrases.english: because something harmful comes out of it —
sometimes the כהן has
less than five quarters [of a kav] of flour,
and he kneads this [flour he received] together with it,
and he thinks his dough has been made fit,
and he comes to eat it while it is still טבל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge to שמואל from step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the case: a special concern (eating טבל) explains the ruling, not a rejection of the gift logic.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה calling the flour 'stolen' proves the giver did not intend a gift, against שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The flour is returned because of a practical danger, so שמואל's gift logic still stands.

steps.title: But everyone knows flour cannot be חלה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer: if people know flour can't be חלה, the כהן would not make that mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't you say that a person knows that one does not separate חלה from flour?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer it just gave in step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole approach in this discussion assumes people know that חלה cannot be taken from flour. If the כהן knows this, he would realize that the flour he received never became חלה. Then he would not think his dough is already exempt.

phrases.english: But didn't you say:
a person knows
that one does not separate חלה from flour!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמְרַתְּ אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין מַפְרִישִׁים חַלָּה קֶמַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 10 that the כהן might think his dough is fixed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Internal contradiction: the sugya assumes people know flour can't be חלה, so the כהן wouldn't be fooled.

steps.title: He knows the rule but not the reason
steps.stepSummary: The כהן knows the rule but misunderstands its reason. He thinks it only protects the כהן from extra work, and he gave up that protection.
steps.simpleTranslation: He knows and he doesn't know. He knows that one doesn't separate חלה from flour, but he doesn't know the reason. He thinks: what is the reason? It is to save the כהן the bother of kneading, and I have given up that right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 11. It splits apart knowing a rule and understanding why the rule exists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The כהן thinks the rule exists only so that he won't have to knead the dough himself. Since he accepted the flour, he thinks he gave up that benefit and the חלה works anyway. So he could still wrongly think his dough is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: The bother of the כהן (the work of kneading)

phrases.english: He knows and he doesn't know.
He knows that one does not separate חלה from flour,
but he does not know [the reason],
for he thinks: what is their reason?
Because of the bother of the כהן,
and as for the bother of the כהן, I have given it up.
phrases.notes: This is the כהן speaking to himself: 'I don't mind doing the kneading.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: knowing the rule versus knowing its reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the כהן knows flour can't be חלה, he couldn't be misled.
steps.terutzMaskana: He knows the rule but wrongly thinks its reason doesn't apply to him, so the mistake is realistic.

steps.title: Why not treat it as תרומה, like the pot case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the כהן can't keep the flour as rabbinic תרומה and take חלה for it from elsewhere, just like the משנה about produce from a pot with a hole.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let it be תרומה, and it should not be eaten until he separates חלה for it from somewhere else. Didn't we learn in a משנה: if one separated from a pot with a hole for a pot without a hole, it is תרומה, but it may not be eaten until he separates תרומה and מעשר for it from somewhere else?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question. Why must the flour be returned at all? There is a known model in another משנה for keeping it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the pot case, the separation did not really work, yet the portion stays with the כהן as תרומה. He just has to fix it by separating again from other produce. The same could work for the flour, which would remove the danger of eating טבל without forcing him to return it.

keyTerms.meaning: A pot with a hole (its plants count as growing from the ground)

phrases.english: But let it be תרומה,
phrases.notes: Here 'תרומה' means the separated flour, which would stay with the כהן.

phrases.english: and it should not be eaten

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיּוֹצִיא עָלֶיהָ חַלָּה מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר.
phrases.english: until he separates חלה for it from somewhere else.
Didn't we learn in a משנה:
[if one separated] from a pot with a hole for one without a hole —
it is תרומה,
and it may not be eaten

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיּוֹצִיא עָלֶיהָ תְּרוּמָה וּמַעֲשֵׂר מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר?
phrases.english: until he separates תרומה and מעשר for it from somewhere else?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling that the flour must be returned, now that the danger from step 10 has been accepted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The requirement that the כהן return the flour.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Comparison to a parallel משנה, where an ineffective separation is kept as תרומה and fixed by separating again from elsewhere.

steps.title: Two pots versus one batch
steps.stepSummary: A כהן will accept the extra separation when there are two clearly separate pots, but not when it is all one batch of flour and dough.
steps.simpleTranslation: With two vessels, he listens. With one vessel, he does not listen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 13 by explaining why the pot case can't be copied for the flour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two pots, the difference is easy to see, so the כהן will accept that he must separate again. Flour and dough from the same batch look like the same thing to him. He won't believe he needs to separate again, so the חכמים made him return the flour instead.
steps.whatToRemember: The flour-חלה is returned because of a practical danger, not because the giver couldn't intend a gift. שמואל's principle still stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the defense of שמואל against רבינא. It shows that חכמים shape a rule around how people will actually behave.

phrases.english: With two vessels — he listens;
phrases.notes: The two pots look clearly different, so the כהן accepts that he has to separate again.

phrases.english: with one vessel — he does not listen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the comparison raised in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the cases based on how people actually behave (two pots versus one batch).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The flour could be kept as תרומה and fixed from elsewhere, like the pot case.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a single batch the כהן won't follow the rule, so the flour must be returned.

steps.title: A second answer: the owner might eat his dough untithed
steps.stepSummary: Really the כהן would listen, but the owner may think his dough is already fixed and eat it as טבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say this: really, the כהן would listen to the rule. The worry is that the owner of the house will think his dough has already been fixed, and he will come to eat it while it is still untithed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a brand-new answer to why the flour must be returned. This time the worry is about the owner of the dough, not the כהן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier answers, the problem was that the כהן might eat untithed dough. Now the גמרא says the כהן would actually follow the rules. The danger is that the owner sees the כהן took 'חלה' and thinks his own dough is done, even though separating from flour does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you want, say': brings in another possible answer
The owner, here the one who gave the flour
His dough has been fixed, meaning the required gifts were already taken
Produce or dough whose required gifts were not yet taken, so it may not be eaten

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two people. Steps 10-14 worried about the כהן eating untithed dough. This new answer worries about the owner eating his own dough untithed.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
Actually, the priest does listen,
but the owner of the house thinks
that his dough has been fixed,
and he will come to eat it untithed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: לְעוֹלָם כֹּהֵן מֵיצָת צָיֵית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the question of steps 13-14 by moving the worry from the כהן to the owner.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shifting the concern to a different person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only reason to return the flour is to protect the כהן from eating untithed dough.
steps.terutzMaskana: The flour is returned so the owner will not think his dough is fixed and eat it as טבל.

steps.title: But the owner knows flour cannot be חלה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: everyone knows חלה is not taken from flour, so the owner would not be fooled.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't you say that a person knows that we do not separate חלה from flour?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new answer using the same point it raised earlier in step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If it is common knowledge that חלה cannot be taken from flour, the owner would realize his dough was never fixed. So why worry that he will eat it as טבל?

keyTerms.meaning: 'But didn't you say': points to an earlier statement to raise a contradiction

phrases.english: But didn't you say: a person knows
that we do not separate חלה from flour!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמְרַתְּ: אָדָם יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁאֵין מַפְרִישִׁין חַלָּה קֶמַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks step 15 with the earlier claim that people know flour cannot be חלה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the owner would think his dough is fixed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If people know חלה cannot come from flour, the owner would not be misled.

steps.title: He knows the rule but not its reason
steps.stepSummary: The owner knows the rule, but thinks it only protects the כהן from extra work, and the כהן agreed to that work.
steps.simpleTranslation: He knows and he doesn't know. He knows that we don't separate חלה from flour, but he doesn't know the reason. He thinks: what is the reason? Because of the כהן's trouble. And the כהן took that trouble upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner knows the rule, but he thinks the reason does not apply here, so he believes his dough is fixed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same answer as step 12, now applied to the owner. He thinks the ban on flour is only there to save the כהן work, like kneading. Since the כהן accepted the flour, the owner thinks the separation counts.

keyTerms.meaning: He knows and does not know: he knows the rule but not its reason
The trouble or extra work of the כהן

phrases.english: He knows and he doesn't know.
He knows that we don't separate חלה from flour,
but he doesn't know,
because he thinks: what is the reason?
Because of the priest's trouble,
and the priest took that trouble upon himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 the same way step 12 answered step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Knowing the rule but misunderstanding its reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Knowing the rule means the owner cannot be misled.
steps.terutzMaskana: He wrongly thinks the reason does not apply, so he believes his dough is fixed.

steps.title: Let it count as תרומה and separate again
steps.stepSummary: Why not let the flour count as rabbinic תרומה and have the owner separate again, as in the משנה about the pot with no hole?
steps.simpleTranslation: So let it be תרומה, and he should separate תרומה again. Didn't we learn in a משנה: if one separates from produce of a pot without a hole for produce of a pot with a hole, it is תרומה, and he must separate תרומה again?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the challenge from step 13, now aimed at the owner. Why not just tell him to separate again?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the separation partly works by rabbinic law, and the person is simply told to separate again. The same could be done here: the flour stays with the כהן, and the owner is told to separate חלה again from his dough.

keyTerms.meaning: And he must separate תרומה again
'Didn't we learn?': introduces a משנה as a challenge
A pot with a hole (counts as growing from the ground) and one without a hole (does not, by Torah law)

phrases.english: So let it be תרומה, and he should separate תרומה again.
Didn't we learn in a משנה:
from a pot without a hole for a pot with a hole,
it is תרומה, and he must separate תרומה again!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיהְוֵי תְּרוּמָה, וְיַחְזוֹר וְיִתְרוֹם. מִי לָא תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises the step 13 challenge again against the new answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need to return the flour
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה shows the הלכה can let a separation count and simply require a second one, so returning the flour seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Two pots yes, one batch no
steps.stepSummary: We already set up that people listen when there are two separate containers, but not with one.
steps.simpleTranslation: We already established: with two containers, he listens. With one container, he does not listen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with the distinction from step 14, now about the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two clearly separate pots, the owner understands that one did not fix the other and will separate again. With flour and dough from the same batch, he will think it is all done and will not separate again.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We have already established': points back to an earlier answer

phrases.english: We already established:
phrases.notes: This points back to the answer in step 14.

phrases.english: with two containers, he listens;
with one container, he does not listen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 with the earlier two-containers distinction.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The pot משנה applies equally to flour and dough.
steps.terutzMaskana: People follow a rule to separate again only when there are two clearly separate containers.

steps.title: The bitter cucumber case shows people do listen
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says a bitter cucumber or spoiled melon is תרומה but one must separate again, even though it is one item.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he doesn't listen? But we learned in a משנה: one who separates a cucumber as תרומה and it turns out bitter, or a melon and it turns out spoiled, it is תרומה, and he must separate תרומה again!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the idea that people won't listen when there is only one container.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cucumber and melon cases have no two separate pots, yet the משנה still says 'it is תרומה, and separate again.' This suggests the rabbis trust people to separate again even without two containers.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But we learned': brings a משנה as a challenge

phrases.english: And he doesn't listen?!
But we learned in a משנה:
one who separates a cucumber as תרומה and it is found bitter,
or a melon and it is found spoiled,
it is תרומה, and he must separate תרומה again!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא צָאֵית?! וְהָתְנַן: הַתּוֹרֵם קִישּׁוּת וְנִמְצָא מָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction of step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that with one container people will not separate again
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The cucumber משנה requires a second separation without two containers, which shows people are trusted to listen.

steps.title: The cucumber is real Torah-level תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The cucumber case is different because the separation is full תרומה by Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is different, because by Torah law it is complete, proper תרומה,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins to answer that the cucumber case is not a fair comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bitter cucumber really is full תרומה by Torah law, so the produce is already fixed by the Torah. Separating again is only an extra rabbinic step, so if someone doesn't listen, no Torah law is broken. With the flour, the separation does nothing, so failing to separate again would mean eating real טבל. The next step gives the source for calling the cucumber real תרומה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'There it is different': separates the cited case from ours

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the rabbis rely on a second separation only when nothing serious is lost if people ignore it.

phrases.english: There it is different,
because by Torah law it is full, proper תרומה,

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי הָתָם, דְּמִדְּאוֹרָיְיתָא תְּרוּמָה מְעַלְּיָא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 by showing how the cucumber case differs.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases by Torah-level status
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cucumber case proves people listen even with one item.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cucumber is full Torah-level תרומה, so a second separation there is only extra; it does not prove people would listen where Torah law is at stake.

steps.title: Proof that bad produce given for good produce is real תרומה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעאי proves from a פסוק that if someone separates תרומה from poor produce for good produce, the תרומה still takes effect by Torah law.
steps.simpleTranslation: We know it from רבי אלעאי. He said: how do we know that someone who separates תרומה from bad produce for good produce has made real תרומה? The פסוק says, 'You shall not bear sin because of it, when you lift up its best part.' If the bad produce did not become holy, why would there be any sin? So we learn that it is real תרומה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is backing up its last answer. It shows the source for the claim that the bitter cucumber is real Torah-level תרומה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah says a person 'bears sin' for not giving the best part. You can only sin through an act that actually worked. If the bad produce did not become תרומה, nothing would have happened and there would be no sin. So the act counts, even though it was done the wrong way.

keyTerms.meaning: One who separates תרומה from poor produce for good produce
His תרומה is valid תרומה (it takes effect)
Bearing sin, being guilty of a wrongdoing
Holy, here meaning it took on the status of תרומה
Literally 'its fat', meaning the best part

steps.whatToRemember: An act can be wrong to do and still take effect. Giving bad produce as תרומה is a sin, yet the תרומה is real by Torah law. That is why the bitter cucumber case is different from the rabbinic cases.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think 'it was a sin, so it doesn't count.' רבי אלעאי's point is the opposite. The sin only exists because it does count.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains Step 21. The cucumber is real Torah-level תרומה, so it is only the rabbis who require separating again, even though it is one item.

phrases.english: From the teaching of Rabbi Ilai.
phrases.notes: This answers an unspoken question: how do we know the cucumber is Torah-level תרומה?

phrases.english: For Rabbi Ilai said:
From where do we know that one who separates תרומה from the bad produce
for the good produce, that his תרומה is תרומה?
As it is said:
"And you shall not bear sin because of it
when you set aside its best part"
If it is not holy,
why would there be any bearing of sin?
From here we learn that one who separates from the bad produce
for the good produce, his תרומה is תרומה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for Step 21's claim that the cucumber is full Torah-level תרומה.
steps.raayaObject: That separating from poor produce for good produce creates real Torah-level תרומה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אלעאי's reading of במדבר 18:32: the 'sin' only makes sense if the תרומה took effect.
